item.title: Hugo Markdown Styling & Formatting Guide
item.dc:creator: Blanket Statement Team
item.description: A comprehensive showcase of typography, code highlighting, tables, quotes, and media formatting available in this Hugo blog starter.
item.content:encoded:
This starter template includes rich formatting support for technical writing, tutorial posts, and personal blogging. Below is a preview of the typography and components.

Headings & Typography

Here is standard body text with bold text, italic text, and inline code.

Subheading Level 3

Paragraph text flows smoothly with readable line heights and carefully tuned margins matching the Blanket Statement visual identity.

Subheading Level 4

Lists are formatted with clean spacing:

  • First bullet point with helpful context
  • Second bullet point with a link to home
  • Third bullet point with embedded sub-items:
    • Sub-item A
    • Sub-item B

Blockquotes

“Productive fidgeting transforms passive listening into active, engaged presence while building something beautiful for others.”

Code Syntax Highlighting

Hugo’s built-in Chroma syntax engine formats code with high contrast:

def knit_square(stitches=30, rows=48):
    """Simulate knitting a 7x9 inch square."""
    fabric = []
    for r in range(rows):
        fabric.append(["knit" for _ in range(stitches)])
    print(f"Finished square with {rows} rows of {stitches} stitches!")
    return fabric

if __name__ == "__main__":
    knit_square()

And in Go / Hugo template syntax:

{{ range where .Site.RegularPages "Section" "posts" }}
  <article>
    <h2>{{ .Title }}</h2>
    <p>{{ .Summary }}</p>
  </article>
{{ end }}

Tables

Metric Target Notes
Block Width 7 inches Standard size
Block Length 9 inches Direction doesn’t matter
Yarn Weight Worsted (#4) Washable acrylic or wool blend
Needle Size US 8 (5.0mm) Provides flexible drape

Image Embeds

Images are automatically responsive with rounded corners and subtle shadows:

Enjoy writing your posts with Hugo!

item.title: Crowdsourcing Warmth: Our Partnership with Project Linus
item.dc:creator: Devorah
item.description: How individual squares from conference attendees around the country are joined together to create blankets for Project Linus.
item.content:encoded:
What happens after you drop off your finished 7” x 9” square at the Pickcode booth?

Every square donated to Blanket Statement becomes part of a larger community quilt. In this post, we take a look behind the scenes at how hundreds of individual contributions become cozy blankets for Project Linus.

About Project Linus

Project Linus is a national non-profit organization that provides handmade blankets to children who are seriously ill, traumatized, or otherwise in need. Since its founding in 1995, Project Linus has delivered more than 10 million blankets nationwide.

The Journey of a Blanket Block

  1. Collection: Squares are gathered from conference participants, logged, and categorized by color palette.
  2. Layout & Arrangement: Volunteers arrange 24 to 35 squares into attractive patchwork designs (usually 4x6 or 5x7 grids).
  3. Seaming: The blocks are crocheted or mattress-stitched together with coordinating yarn.
  4. Bordering: A clean decorative border (single crochet or crab stitch) is added around the perimeter for durability and finish.
  5. Quality Check & Labeling: Each blanket receives an official Project Linus label and is inspected for safety (secure tails, softness, washability).
  6. Delivery: Local chapters deliver the blankets to pediatric hospitals, shelters, and crisis centers.
+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |  7x9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+
      --> Finished 36" x 45" Blanket!

How You Can Help Beyond the Conference

Can’t attend in person? You can knit or crochet blocks at home and mail them to us, or start a Blanket Statement chapter at your own local meetup or school!

item.title: A Beginner's Guide to Knitting 7” x 9” Squares
item.dc:creator: Devorah
item.description: Everything you need to know about casting on, garter stitch, gauge, and completing your first blanket block.
item.content:encoded:
Never held a pair of knitting needles before? No problem! Knitting a 7” x 9” blanket block is the single best starter project. There are no complicated increases or decreases—just a straightforward rectangle worked in classic Garter Stitch.

Materials Needed

  • Yarn: 1 skein worsted weight (medium #4) acrylic or washable wool.
  • Needles: US Size 8 (5.0 mm) or Size 9 (5.5 mm).
  • Ruler: The ruler printed on the ball band, or any standard measuring tape.
  • Tapestry Needle: To weave in your yarn ends.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Step 1: Cast On

Cast on approximately 28 to 34 stitches (depending on your needle size and yarn tension).

[ Needle ] ===o===o===o===o===o===o===o=== [ Cast on 30 sts ]

Tip: Measure your cast-on row against the ball band ruler. If it is 7 inches wide, you are ready to knit!

Step 2: The Garter Stitch

Every single row is worked in the knit stitch:

  1. Insert right needle into the front of the first stitch from left to right.
  2. Wrap working yarn counter-clockwise around the right needle.
  3. Pull the new loop through and slide the old stitch off the left needle.
  4. Repeat across the row!

Step 3: Knit Until 9 Inches

Continue knitting every row until the piece measures 9 inches from your cast-on edge. (Note: 9” x 7” is also fine—direction doesn’t matter!)

Step 4: Bind Off

  1. Knit two stitches.
  2. Use the left needle to lift the first stitch over the second stitch and off the needle.
  3. Knit the next stitch and repeat until one loop remains.
  4. Cut the yarn leaving a 6-inch tail, pull through the loop, and tighten.

Ready to Turn In Your Square?

Bring your completed block to the Pickcode booth at the conference, or email us at blanketstatementproject@gmail.com for shipping instructions!

item.title: The Science of Productive Fidgeting
item.dc:creator: Blanket Statement Team
item.description: Exploring cognitive research on motor movement, attention span, working memory, and why tactile tasks enhance listening.
item.content:encoded:
Why do so many educators, engineers, and researchers knit during long seminars? Is it a distraction, or is it actually a powerful tool for deep listening?

Cognitive science has increasingly validated what craft enthusiasts have known intuitively for decades: low-intensity tactile activity can significantly enhance working memory and auditory retention.

The Yerkes-Dodson Law and Arousal Regulation

The Yerkes-Dodson Law describes the relationship between psychological arousal and cognitive performance:

Performance
  ^
  |        Optimal Focus
  |            /\
  |           /  \
  |          /    \
  |  Under-        Over-
  |  arousal       arousal
  +------------------------> Arousal Level

When sitting still during a passive lecture, the brain’s baseline arousal drops, leading to daydreaming or the impulse to check one’s phone. Repetitive micro-movements—like forming a knit stitch—provide just enough sensory stimulation to keep the nervous system in the optimal focus zone without overloading working memory.

Tactile Motion vs. Digital Multi-Tasking

Research contrasting tactile crafts with digital smartphone usage reveals a crucial distinction:

Activity Working Memory Load Visual / Linguistic Interference Retention Impact
Knitting / Crocheting Low (Automatic motor loop) Minimal Positive (+15–20%)
Doodling Low Low Positive (+29%)
Smartphone Scrolling High Severe (Linguistic conflict) Negative (-40%)
Sitting Motionless Variable Mind-wandering risk Baseline

A famous 2009 study by psychologist Jackie Andrade demonstrated that participants who doodled while listening to a monotonous telephone message retained 29% more information than non-doodlers. Knitting operates on identical neurological pathways.

Summary

Next time you pull out yarn and needles during a keynote, know that you are actively optimizing your brain for learning—and creating a warm blanket for a child in need at the same time.

item.title: Welcome to Blanket Statement
item.dc:creator: Devorah
item.description: Why we started Blanket Statement and how we are turning conference fidgeting into warm blankets for children in need.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Blanket Statement!

If you’ve ever attended an all-day conference, faculty meeting, or professional development workshop, you know how hard it can be to sit motionless for hours at a time. Many of us are kinesthetic learners: we need our hands engaged in rhythmic, low-cognitive-load activity to keep our minds alert and receptive.

“Folks who knit or crochet when attending talks and meetings do so in order to help maintain focus on the talk. Using our hands keeps our brains from wandering from the speaker.”

The Conference Dilemma

We’ve all seen attendees staring at their smartphones during presentations. While some might be live-tweeting or taking notes, many are checking email, reading news, or scrolling through feeds — activities that actively compete for cognitive attention and pull focus away from the speaker.

Knitting and crocheting do the exact opposite. Because the hand movements are repetitive and tactile, they satisfy the urge to fidget without drawing linguistic or analytical brain processing away from the presenter.

Crowdsourcing Comfort

Instead of just knitting for ourselves, Blanket Statement turns every conference hour into something tangible: 7" x 9" knitted or crocheted squares that are seamed together into blankets for Project Linus, an organization providing security and comfort blankets to children who are ill, traumatized, or in need.

How You Can Participate

  1. Stop by the Pickcode Booth: Grab a skein of yarn, a set of needles, or a crochet hook.
  2. Knit or Crochet During Talks: Work on your 7" x 9" block throughout the day.
  3. Drop Off & Tag: Bring your completed square back to the booth, fill out a donor tag, and celebrate your contribution!

We are thrilled to embark on this journey with you. Check back on this blog for progress updates, square counts, and helpful crafting tutorials!
